tier_reason: Independent third-party run (mxmlnkn, 2025-08-05, zlib-ng discussion 871) with zlib-ng's public deflatebench harness on Silesia-small.tar, 15 runs trim worst 5, AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, GCC 13.3.0, Ubuntu 24.04.2, comparing zlib-rs 0.5.1 with stock zlib. Not A: build flags for the zlib-rs CLI and for zlib are not stated, and the zlib-rs side ran through an AI-generated flate2 CLI rather than a documented build.

corrections.claimed_speedup: zlib-ng discussion 871, run by mxmlnkn on 2025-08-05 (deflatebench, single-file mode, Silesia-small.tar): level 9 compress zlib-rs 0.493 s vs stock zlib 2.106 s (4.3x, derived from page data) at ratio 40.409% vs 40.490%; level 9 decompress 0.027 s vs 0.099 s (3.7x, derived from page data); level 6 compress 0.264 s vs 1.149 s (4.4x, derived from page data) at 41.032% vs 40.734%. The comment's generated-mode summary puts libdeflate, ISA-L, zlib-rs and zlib-ng at about 3x faster than zlib in decompression, and the author says zlib-rs is 'equally fast' as zlib-ng on his system, not faster. README: performance generally on par with zlib-ng.
corrections.caveats: Rust implementation, usable from C++ through the libz-rs-sys C ABI (cdylib). The independent run measured zlib-rs through an AI-generated Rust CLI using flate2 with the zlib-rs backend, not through the C ABI. zlib-rs follows zlib-ng's implementation: its level-1 and level-9 outputs on Silesia-small.tar are byte-identical in size to zlib-ng's (8,526,745 and 6,358,951 bytes) and its times match zlib-ng's, so the win over zlib is zlib-ng's design. At level 1 its ratio is much worse than stock zlib's (54.185% vs 44.805%), so level-1 speed is not ratio-matched. Search snippets report zlib-rs 6-10%+ faster than zlib-ng at decompression for 1 KB to 65 KB chunks (Trifecta blog 'zlib-rs is faster than C', blocked, snippet only); the independent run saw parity.

notes: Numbers verified on discussion 871; tier B holds. Fold call: separate Rust code base, but ISRG commissioned it as an implementation based on zlib-ng and it reproduces zlib-ng's output and speed, so under the ports rule it folds into zlib-ng as a duplicate (memory-safe drop-in port); if kept separately, B is the right tier. Metadata confirmed: Zlib license, 698 stars, 60 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-09-17.

tier_reason: First-party README and etc/BENCHMARKS.md tables against bzip2, xz/lzma, gzip and zstd with command lines and timings, but no CPU model, compiler or flags (only 'x64 Linux clang13 builds usually' in a general note), and no benchmark harness beyond shell commands.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Perl 5 tarball: bzip3 -b 511 546,456,978 bytes vs xz 2,056,645,240, zstd 3,076,143,660, bzip2 3,441,163,911; wall-clock decompression bzip3 (parallel) 4 min 06 s, xz 4 min 40 s, zstd 3 min 51 s, bzip2 9 min 22 s (about 2.3x faster than bzip2 and 1.14x faster than xz, slower than zstd; derived from page data). Compression wall clock: bzip3 -j 12 7:10 vs bzip2 -9 17:16 vs xz -T16 -9 12:09 vs zstd -T12 -16 6:35. etc/BENCHMARKS.md Silesia, one thread: bzip3 -b 16 17.5 s to 47,227,855 bytes vs lzma -9 77.2 s to 48,761,670 and zstd -19 83.5 s to 53,000,145 (about 4.4x faster than lzma -9 and 4.8x faster than zstd -19 at a smaller output; derived from page data). Single-threaded, bzip3 compresses slower than bzip2: Calgary 265 ms vs 173 ms, Linux tar 77.4 s vs 61.6 s.
corrections.caveats: First party. Hardware, compiler and flags not stated; README says performance depends heavily on the compiler (clang13 x64 about 17 MiB/s compress, 23 MiB/s decompress per thread). The speed win over bzip2 on the Perl tarball comes from parallelism (bzip3 -j 12 vs single-threaded bzip2; parallel decode vs bzip2's single thread, on an HDD); one-thread compression is slower than bzip2 in etc/BENCHMARKS.md (Calgary, Linux). The defensible win is ratio plus speed against xz/lzma -9 and zstd -19 at high ratio. Issue #2 ('Better performance' claim, 2022, closed) reported bzip3 noticeably slower than bzip2 in quick tests, without numbers. LGPL-3.0 only; libsais and LZP parts Apache-2.0.

notes: README numbers match the record. Re-framed the speed claim: against bzip2 it is a multithreading win, against xz/lzma -9 and zstd -19 it is faster at a better ratio on Silesia. Metadata confirmed: LGPL-3.0, 1.5k stars, 66 forks, not archived, last commit 2026-09-09.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the benchmark code is public (examples/bench_suite.rs driven by scripts/bench_aws_suite.sh, results in docs/benchmarks/suite-2026-09-21.md and benchmarks/suite/), compiler rustc 1.98 with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' and a release profile of opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, and CPU models Graviton3 (Neoverse V1, c7g.2xlarge) and Xeon Platinum 8488C (c7i.2xlarge), against in-process libzstd 1.5.7 and LZ4. A rests on the one-thread zstd comparison; the LZ4 and 8-thread rows are weaker (see caveats).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Suite 2026-09-21 (8.7 GB corpus of logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet), one thread, MB/s: Glyd --max ratio 3.98 decompresses 1,571 vs zstd -3 (ratio 3.86) 1,425 on Graviton3 (1.10x) but 1,287 vs 1,518 on Sapphire Rapids (0.85x, slower), and compresses at 233 vs 313 and 266 vs 377. Glyd default (ratio 2.82) decompresses 3,309 on Graviton3 and 2,752 on Sapphire Rapids vs LZ4 (ratio 2.72) 1,394 and 1,206, compressing at 332 vs 504 and 327 vs 456. Eight threads: Glyd default decompresses 22,707 MB/s and --max 10,413 vs zstd -3 1,422 and LZ4 1,392, but zstd and LZ4 frames are decoded on one thread. README summary: reads 3-7x faster than zstd on a server, writes at 0.71-0.77x zstd -3's speed.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', cargo release profile opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1; baselines libzstd 1.5.7 via the zstd crate (bulk API, in-process) and LZ4 via the lz4 crate's frame encoder/decoder; zstd 1.5.5 and lz4 1.9.4 CLIs from Ubuntu 24.04 for CLI rows.
corrections.hardware: AWS c7g.2xlarge (Graviton3, Neoverse V1, 8 vCPU) and c7i.2xlarge (Sapphire Rapids, Xeon Platinum 8488C, 8 vCPU), Ubuntu 24.04
corrections.caveats: First party, very young repo (240 stars, 1 fork) with sweeping claims. Like-for-like (one thread, similar ratio) the decode win over zstd -3 is small and platform-dependent: 1.10x on Graviton3, 0.85x (slower) on Sapphire Rapids, and compression is slower than zstd -3 on both. The 22.7 GB/s headline compares 8-thread Glyd decoding with single-thread zstd/LZ4 frame decoding. The LZ4 baseline in examples/bench_suite.rs uses the lz4 crate's streaming frame Decoder with read_to_end, not the LZ4 block API, which likely explains LZ4 decoding at only about 1.4 GB/s; the README's 'each codec on its fastest API' does not hold for LZ4, so the LZ4 decode comparison is weak. Glyd writes a per-block checksum; zstd frames here carry none. Store and GPU parts are BUSL-1.1 (non-commercial free).

notes: README and suite numbers match the record; methodology is fully documented, so tier rises to A on the one-thread zstd rows, but the honest single-core result is mixed (faster on Graviton3, slower on Sapphire Rapids at --max); the decode lead over LZ4 rests on a frame-reader baseline. Codec license BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0-only (Cargo.toml), usability mixed because of BUSL store/GPU; last commit 2026-10-03 confirmed.
